meta.title: Banning non-compete clauses for low- and middle-income workers (2025-26 Budget)
meta.summary: Real policy: the ban on non-compete clauses for employees earning below the Fair Work Act high-income threshold, announced on 25 March 2025 with the 2025-26 Budget, and Treasury's preferred option in its Impact Analysis (OIA, 21 September 2026). The reforms apply prospectively, to new and varied employment contracts, from 2027. The burden proposal holds the Impact Analysis's familiarisation costs for Options 2 and 3; the labour lever follows the Productivity Commission's 2024 non-compete simulation, which Treasury cites. Treasury's own GDP figure is the PC's $5.1 billion.

burden.title: Non-compete clauses and other worker restraints: familiarisation costs (Treasury Impact Analysis, 2026)
burden.description: The Impact Analysis's regulatory burden estimate (Table 4), rebuilt from its stated inputs (Tables 5 and 6, p. 52). Option 3 reproduces Treasury's $16.3 million; Option 2 comes to about $48.9 million against Treasury's $46.4 million, because Treasury's $7.5 million and $0.7 million for medium and large businesses are less than three times its Option 3 figures although Option 2's time is three times as long (90 minutes against 30).

options.name: Option 2: partial ban (preferred)
options.description: Ban non-compete clauses for employees earning below the Fair Work Act high-income threshold ($183,100), ban co-worker non-solicitation clauses, no-poach and wage-fixing agreements, and limit the remaining restraints (a 6-month limit on non-competes above the threshold; no cascading clauses). 90 minutes of familiarisation (IA Table 5).

nonCompetes.coveredShareChange.note: A ban removes the coverage of the one in five workers bound by a non-compete (−0.2, the PC's simulation). Option 2 keeps non-competes, for up to 6 months, above the high-income threshold; Treasury expects it to deliver at least 90% of a full ban's increase in job mobility, so the low end of the change is 90% of −0.2.

source.description: Treasury, Impact Analysis: Non-compete clauses and other worker restraints (OIA, published 21 September 2026), p. 41 (PDF p. 44)

competition.alternatives: Option 1, the status quo: the common law restraint of trade doctrine, with the NSW Restraints of Trade Act still applying to NSW contracts. Option 3, a full ban of all employment restraints of trade, including non-competes for high-income employees and client non-solicitation clauses. Treasury preferred Option 2: it is more targeted, leaving businesses able to use reasonable non-competes for high-income employees and client non-solicitation clauses to protect legitimate interests, and so to invest in training and other assets; Option 3's mobility gains would be larger but it would give businesses no flexibility (IA pp. 27 and 62).
competition.benefits: Higher wages and job mobility: workers at firms that use non-competes extensively are paid about 4% less (e61), and job mobility could rise by 1–2 percentage points; Option 2 delivers at least 90% of a full ban's increase (IA summary; p. 41). More entrepreneurship and new businesses, knowledge spillovers, lower litigation costs (Option 3 saves up to $17 million a year), and consumer prices about 0.1% lower in the PC's modelling (IA summary; pp. 48–49).
